Question

<column-break/>

Article 3: Whether the more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third article, the procedure is as follows: It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because things that are prior by nature are posterior and less known to us, but universals are prior by nature. Furthermore, composite things are prior to us compared to simple things, but universals are simple; therefore, they are known later to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, *Physics* I</note> says that the defined <note>term: *diffinitum* <gloss>the thing defined</gloss></note> falls into our cognition before the parts of the definition, and parts of a definition are less universal; for instance, "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," yet universals are known later to us. Furthermore, we encounter effects and causes and principles <unclear>by chance</unclear>, but universals are known later to us. But if it is true that, as stated in the first book of the *Physics*, we proceed from the whole to the singulars, I respond that it must be said that in our intellectual cognition, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition takes its origin in some way from sensory cognition. And because sense is of singulars, while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars is prior to us than the cognition of universals. Second, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And what proceeds from potency to act arrives first at the incomplete act, which is midway between pure potency and perfect act. The perfect act, to which the intellect arrives, is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known as being in act and in a certain way in potency. As it is said in the first book of the *Physics*, what is first manifest and certain to us is more confused. Afterward, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained within it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, a whole, or that in which parts are contained in potency, and an integral whole can be known; for both wholes can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing: just as knowing "animal" indistinctly versus knowing the animal in which rationality or irrationality exists, which is knowing a man or a lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect first to know "animal" and to know "man." And if I compare any thing, whether more or less, just as sense goes from potency to act, so does the intellect. Such is the order

<column-break/>

of cognition appearing in sense. For in sense, we distinguish more, and when less is known, it is through being more remote by <unclear>corporeal being</unclear>, and <unclear>being</unclear> and "animal"; and more <unclear>observed</unclear> is "being animal," and <unclear>observed</unclear> is "good" and prior is "good" and "being." Or it pleases, and it is clear that a child from the beginning first distinguishes "good" and "not-good"; and children at the beginning call all men "father." Afterward, however, they determine each one, as stated in the first book of the *Physics*: it is manifest that one knows something indistinctly while it is still in potency, whether one knows the fiction or the principle; thus, one knows the genus and has the power to know the species. And so, by itself, indistinct cognition is the medium between potency and act. And thus the cognition of singulars is prior to us, and the cognition of the universal is sensory cognition and intellectual cognition. If there is both sense and intellect, the cognition of the more universal is prior to the cognition of the lesser and common. As for the first objection, that can be considered in a double way. One way is considering the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and the true itself have a relationship to many things, the abstraction of the intellect is the end of this mode, while the truth is posterior. As in the first book *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle, *De Anima*</note>, the universal is either nothing or is posterior; but <unclear>Plato</unclear> posited universals as substances. And in this consideration, it is true, because particulars do not exist except by participation in the subsistent universals which are called "ideas." In another way, it can be considered according to the nature itself of animality or humanity, as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a double order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, when those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. In this way, the more universal is prior in nature, which appears manifest in the generation of man and animal. For the animal is generated before the man, as stated in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature, and that which is perfect is prior to that which is imperfect; and in this way, the less universal is prior in nature, for the nature of man is not arrested in the generation of the animal, but intends to generate a man. As for the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole is to a part; for the whole that is more universal contains not only the man and the horse, but it also contains the less universal, and it holds within it not only the more universal but others as well, just as "animal" contains not only man but also the rational. Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition than "man," if "man" is prior in our cognition, then "animal" is so because of its reason. As for the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is a house. In another way, when it is parts of this whole, and stones; it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we know the house with a certain confusion. Thus, it must be said that the thing defined, considered absolutely, is prior to us and is defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be notified by those things, but rather, those things are the parts.

<summary>This page contains the third article of a question regarding the nature of intellectual cognition, specifically addressing the priority of universal versus singular knowledge in the human mind, and distinguishing between orders of generation and orders of perfection.</summary>
